content: In the second phase of the search for randomized controlled trials (RCTs), 4,882 references were identified. Of these, 4,871 were excluded based on their titles due to irrelevance or because they did not involve children. Among the remaining 14 references, three were duplicates and were removed. Of the remaining 11 references, 10 were excluded after abstract review for not meeting inclusion criteria, leaving one study that was fully reviewed and met the inclusion criteria. An expanded search identified 17 additional references, of which three were duplicates and one had already been identified in the second-phase search. This left 13 abstracts for review, of which seven did not meet inclusion criteria. The remaining six full-text references were assessed, and four were excluded, leaving two studies that met the inclusion criteria. These two studies had previously been excluded during the second-phase search due to their short duration (three weeks) and lack of random allocation to treatment groups. Eighteen additional references were excluded based on abstract screening for not meeting basic inclusion criteria. Missing data were retrieved by contacting Dr. Dawn Wilson, who provided additional information regarding her studies. All included studies were published in English. Three controlled trials were conducted in the United States, while one cohort study was conducted in the Netherlands. Two RCTs recruited children through schools or a combination of schools, churches, and advertisements. The non-randomized trial recruited participants from an existing twin panel, and the cohort study followed children prospectively for seven years. The two RCTs included a total of 250 participants. The non-randomized trial included 76 participants aged 11–14 years. Interventions in the studies varied. One RCT involved dietary education, behavioral skills training, and performance feedback over three weeks. The other two controlled trials provided potassium and placebo supplements, with durations of four weeks and three years, respectively. There were insufficient studies to evaluate the differential effects of potassium intake at various levels. No studies meeting inclusion criteria reported the effects of increased potassium on blood lipids, catecholamine levels, or other minor side effects in children. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. The cohort study evidence was not downgraded but was inherently of low quality due to study design limitations. Overall, the body of evidence was at risk of serious bias, with issues such as lack of randomization, inadequate blinding, and high attrition rates in some studies.
